_comment: Drives TfLiteModelManager / TfLiteProcessor. Nothing about these graphs is
hardcoded in Kotlin: input width/height/channels, tensor data type and any
quantisation scale/zero-point are read from the .tflite flatbuffer itself at
runtime via Interpreter.getInputTensor/getOutputTensor. Only the things a
TFLite graph cannot describe live here - how pixels are normalised before
the first op, how the head's numbers turn into years, and the class order.
Add a variant or swap a file and no Kotlin has to change.

face_crop._comment: Fraction of the detected face box added on each side before cropping. These heads want a looser, UTKFace-style crop that includes hair and chin; the raw YuNet box is tighter than that. 0.15 measured best - see _calibration below.

_calibration: These graphs ship with no TFLite metadata describing their input scaling or
their age target, so the values below were measured rather than guessed: the
age head was run over six faces under every plausible combination of pixel
scaling (x/255, x/127.5-1, per-image standardization, raw), crop margin
(0.00 / 0.15 / 0.30) and age scale (100 / 116), and each combination was
scored by mean absolute error against what the MiVOLO model in this same app
predicts for the same photographs. Result, best first:
per-image standardization      ->  MAE 25+ and wildly unstable across margins
MAE ~8 against MiVOLO is the expected gap for a 400 KB head measured against a
100 MB one, not a sign of a decode error: the alternatives are 3-6x worse.

age._comment: mean 0 / std 1 over pixel_scale 255 is a plain x/255, which is what the graph was trained on - it starts at a depthwise conv with no normalisation layer of its own.

decode._comment: output[0] is a single unactivated scalar; the training target was age / 100.
The graph ends in SOFTMAX, so the output is already a probability vector; TfLiteProcessor renormalises only if it is not.
